 Twenty-eight hippos dead. Floating carcasses clogging the Semuliki River. Another grim reminder that Africa's oldest national park is fighting a battle on multiple fronts. 
 An anthrax outbreak has ripped through Virunga National Park in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, killing dozens of iconic hippopotamuses. If you think this is just an isolated wildlife tragedy, look closer. When a deadly pathogen hits a war-torn region already suffering from severe environmental stress and political instability, the consequences go way beyond park borders. 
 The Science Behind the Spores
 Let's get real about what Bacillus anthracis actually does. Anthrax isn't a modern virus or a fleeting infection. It is a stubborn, spore-forming bacterium that can lurk silently in deserted soil for decades. 
 When dry spells hit and vegetation dries up, herbivores face a brutal choice. They can starve, or they can graze right down to the dirt, ingesting the dormant spores trapped in the dust and mud. That's exactly what's happening around the water points of Virunga. 
 Hippos aren't just large animals taking up space. They're critical ecosystem engineers. Joël Mbusa Mapoli, an expert in ecology and veterinary medicine, points out that these animals drive nutrient flows across aquatic and terrestrial boundaries. When hippos die en masse, the entire landscape feels the shockwave. 
 A Repeating Nightmare
 This isn't a one-off event. Just last year, an anthrax outbreak claimed the lives of 65 hippos in the exact same park. Park rangers and conservationists had to mobilize heavy machinery like excavators just to pull heavy carcasses out of the water to prevent further contamination.

 With Virunga's total hippo population estimated at over 2,700 across 171 groups based on recent census data, losing 28 animals in a single month represents a massive hit. It cuts straight into the population stability that conservationists have spent decades trying to build up after past poaching crises.
 The Human Danger Zone
 The real hazard goes beyond animal conservation. Anthrax is a zoonotic disease, meaning it jumps easily from animals to humans. 
 Park management has issued urgent warnings to local communities living near the Semuliki River and Lake Edward. Handling dead wildlife, skinning carcasses, or eating bushmeat infected with the bacteria puts human lives directly in the crosshairs. In past flare-ups across the broader North Kivu landscape, suspected human cases and fatalities have shadowed wildlife mortality spikes.

 Yet telling struggling local communities not to harvest available meat is easier said than done, especially when food security is constantly threatened by regional conflict. 
 Conflict Constrains Conservation
 You can't talk about Virunga without talking about the war. For nearly three decades, armed conflict has plagued eastern DRC, fueling deforestation and rampant poaching. 
 According to park authorities, conservation teams have lost direct control over a substantial chunk of the park's territory over the last four years due to ongoing fighting between the Congolese army and M23 insurgent groups. When rangers can't patrol safely, monitoring wildlife health becomes nearly impossible. Quick responses to outbreaks turn into slow-motion disasters because communication lines are severed and areas are locked down by militia activity.

 Environmental activist Olivier Ndoole Bahemuke notes that prolonged insecurity completely shreds the institutional safety nets meant to protect both people and nature. 
 What Needs to Happen Now
 Containment requires more than just crossing fingers and hoping for rain. Local authorities, the Congolese Institute for the Conservation of Nature, and health ministries must maintain active surveillance loops around the affected rivers. Carcasses need immediate, safe disposal before spores spread further into the soil or water table. 
 Protecting Virunga means recognizing that wildlife health, human health, and political stability are tied together. Ignore one, and the whole system collapses.
